With guardrails (PII redaction, citations to authoritative docs, read-only tool use, sandbox validation, and change-control), teams commonly save 15–60 minutes per ticket or 20–40% on routine installs/troubleshooting (approximately $25–$150 at $50–$150/hr) while maintaining expert-level quality via human review and explicit validation tests (before/after baselines, config diffing, and security scans).
gpt5_risks_types: Security, Privacy, Misinformation, Malicious actors and Misuse
gpt5_risks_justifications: This task is safety‑critical: incorrect installation or configuration guidance can disable protections, create exploitable exposures, or cause outages and data loss. Using an LLM with a human engineer increases risk via (a) confident but wrong commands, paths, or policy settings; (b) insecure defaults or omission of environment‑specific hardening steps; (c) capability‑induced oversight—fluent, specific outputs can cause engineers or end users to defer and copy‑paste without full verification; (d) privacy/secret leakage when logs, configs, or keys are pasted into the model or retained in chat; (e) prompt‑injection from error messages or linked docs that steer the model to disable controls or fetch/run untrusted scripts; and (f) misuse—attackers can use the same system to craft evasion techniques or social‑engineering scripts. Many failures are subtle and only surface under attack, making them hard to detect reliably unless every step is checked against authoritative vendor documentation and tested in a sandbox; tool‑using agents (shell/RMM/integration access) further increase blast radius.

Title: Digital Forensics Analysts
Task: Adhere to legal policies and procedures related to handling digital media.
gpt5_rewards_justifications: Moderate rewards when used as a co-pilot for documentation and compliance support rather than as a source of legal advice: generate chain-of-custody checklists aligned to current SOPs, draft warrant/scope summaries from verified inputs, normalize and cross-reference policy citations, compare recorded steps to procedural requirements, produce templated affidavits/intake forms, and assemble auditor-ready logs. Savings mainly come from faster paperwork and fewer reworks: typically 10–45 minutes per matter (about $10–$90 at $60–$120/hr) and occasionally 1–2 hours on lengthy reports ($60–$240), assuming all legal points are cross-checked against up-to-date statutes, case law, and agency SOPs with human QA. Additional gains from automated PII tagging and redaction suggestions for disclosure. Net reward is moderate because verification and secure deployment (on-prem models, redaction pipelines, RBAC, audit trails) offset part of the speedup.
gpt5_risks_types: Misinformation, Privacy, Security, Malicious actors and Misuse
gpt5_risks_justifications: Safety-critical. Errors in chain-of-custody, warrant scope, imaging procedures, or evidence handling can lead to suppression of evidence, wrongful outcomes, or civil liability. LLMs can hallucinate or misstate jurisdiction-specific law, standards (e.g., Daubert/Frye), or agency SOPs, and may be out-of-date. Their confident, legal-sounding guidance increases automation bias, so analysts may defer and reduce independent verification (capability-induced oversight risk). Uploading or summarizing digital evidence with public or non-compliant LLMs risks unlawful exposure of PII/PHI/CSAM/attorney–client materials (privacy) and leakage via logs or model training. Agentic or tool-using setups can be prompt-injected by content extracted from evidence, exfiltrating data or triggering unsafe actions; misconfiguration could even write to evidence media or alter metadata (security/integrity). Adversaries could craft documents to manipulate LLM-driven workflows (misuse). Compared to human-only processes, naive use of LLMs can roughly double the chance that a subtle procedural error or omission escapes review (e.g., on the order of a 20–50% relative increase), whereas with strict controls—no raw evidence to public models, model use limited to drafting/checklists, mandatory cross-checks against current statutes/SOPs, and full auditability—the incremental risk can likely be kept to a low single-digit percentage.

Title: Digital Forensics Analysts

gpt5_risks_types: Misinformation, Privacy, Security, Malicious actors and Misuse, Discrimination
gpt5_risks_justifications: Safety-critical: attribution informs containment, legal action, notifications, and may affect individuals or organizations’ reputations. LLMs increase risk by producing confident but incorrect attributions (e.g., hallucinated links to known threat actors, shaky IP geolocation inferences, misread timelines), and by omitting or mis-weighting evidence in large, noisy logs—issues that can be hard to detect at scale. Capability-induced oversight risk is significant: polished ATT&CK mappings and coherent narratives can prompt analysts to defer to model output and perform less exhaustive verification. Logs may contain attacker-controlled strings that can manipulate agentic systems (prompt injection), trigger unsafe tool actions, or exfiltrate data. Handling logs often implicates sensitive PII, credentials, or proprietary data; using non-compliant cloud LLMs risks disclosure or retention. Integrations expand the attack surface (tokens, connectors, code execution). Bias can creep into attribution (e.g., language, TTP stereotypes) leading to discriminatory or unfounded country/actor claims. Attackers can also craft false flags tailored to mislead LLM-driven workflows. While careful, evidentiary verification and chain-of-custody checks can catch many issues, they are costly and models’ persuasiveness makes rare but high-impact errors more likely to slip through.

Title: Digital Forensics Analysts

gpt5_risks_types: Security, Privacy, Misinformation, Malicious actors and Misuse

Title: Digital Forensics Analysts
Task: Create system images or capture network settings from information technology environments to preserve as evidence.
gpt5_rewards_justifications: Rewards are mainly in guidance and documentation, not execution: generate tailored checklists, recall command syntax and tool options across platforms, draft chain‑of‑custody forms and acquisition notes, and scaffold automation scripts for repeatable collections—while the analyst validates every step and runs tools in a controlled, offline, compliant environment. Imaging time is dominated by I/O and established SOPs, so net savings are modest (often 5–20 minutes per host/device for setup/documentation, roughly $10–$60 at $60–$180/hr). With strict no‑PII prompts, offline/on‑prem models, and mandatory verification against lab playbooks, quality can match expert‑only workflows, but gains remain limited.
gpt5_risks_types: Misinformation, Privacy, Security, Malicious actors and Misuse
gpt5_risks_justifications: Safety‑critical: preservation errors can irreversibly alter or invalidate evidence and jeopardize cases. LLMs raise risk by suggesting incomplete or unsafe acquisition steps (e.g., imaging without a write‑blocker, mounting RW, missing unallocated/slack space, failing to hash/verify with SHA‑256, omitting volatile memory, using lossy compression, or capturing only partial network state such as missing IPv6, VPN, VLAN, DNS, DHCP, ARP, routing, and firewall info). Highly fluent step‑by‑steps increase automation bias, so analysts may defer and skip independent verification. Privacy/Security risks are acute: sharing any case details or artifacts with non‑compliant models could leak PHI/C JI/PII or proprietary data; chain‑of‑custody metadata, credentials, or network topology; models may retain data or route it cross‑border, violating HIPAA/CJIS/GDPR or enterprise policy. Agentic use increases prompt‑injection and tool‑escape risk from hostile artifacts (e.g., logs/scripts that instruct the agent to mount disks RW, run chkdsk, clear caches, or alter timestamps) or from compromised web pages/tools. Capability‑induced oversight risk: because models can produce correct‑looking, tool‑ and OS‑specific commands (dd/dc3dd, FTK Imager, ewfacquire, netsh/nmcli/tcpdump, esxcli, aws ec2 create‑snapshot, etc.), analysts may over‑trust subtle but harmful defaults (e.g., missing conv=noerror,sync; wrong block size; imaging a mounted logical volume instead of the physical device; failing to disable TRIM; skipping BitLocker/APFS metadata; not capturing firmware/NVRAM; not preserving router/switch configs and logs; inadequate hash logging and time sync), leading to undetected integrity gaps.

Because frontier LLMs produce polished, standard-sounding playbooks, analysts may defer to them and reduce independent verification (capability-induced oversight risk). Additional risks: privacy leakage if case details are sent to non-compliant services; prompt injection or data poisoning from suspect-provided artifacts leading the model/agent to reveal secrets or propose unsafe steps; model output that over-targets certain individuals or devices based on biased priors. Compared with human-only planning, the combined LLM+expert setup can plausibly raise the probability that a material planning defect escapes review by roughly 20–50% absent strict controls; with strict verification against authoritative procedures and counsel, this uplift can be reduced but not eliminated.

Capability‑induced oversight risk is high because polished drafts reduce scrutiny; subtle defects are hard to spot without line‑by‑line source tracing to NIST/ISO/SWGDE/ACPO and applicable laws. Compared to human‑only drafting, the LLM+expert workflow can increase the probability that a material compliance/admissibility defect escapes review by roughly 1.5–2× (e.g., from approximately 1–3% to approximately 2–6% per major policy revision) if teams accept uncited passages or fail to perform authoritative cross‑checks; privacy/security exposure also rises if non‑hardened systems are used.

Task: Duplicate digital evidence to use for data recovery and analysis procedures.
